title: Pulse-echo benchmark scratch — cache reverb & recovery
content:
Purpose: quick sketch of a "pulse-echo" microburst benchmark variant — goal is to measure how warm-cache state + short high-intensity pulses affect tail latency and recovery time. Wanted a lightweight, reproducible playground before writing a formal test harness.

Context and motivation:
- We keep seeing short 2–6s client-side bursts in prod that create a tail shock and slow warm-cache recovery. Ops sees higher p99 for ~10–30s after a spike. Hypothesis: cache priming + request interleaving policies interact badly with preemption and batching windows.
- This experiment is intentionally small: single-node (8xA100 emulation), one model shard, synthetic payloads (short seq len ~64 token), and varying inter-pulse idle.

Setup (notes to self):
- Binary used: bench/pulse-echo-v0 (local harness) — wraps loadgen and injects background 'echo' probes.
- Model: llama-13b-8bit-quant (toy config) — consistent kv cache behavior.
- Worker config: concurrency cap = 12, batch timeout = 8ms, batching window = flexible, preemption enabled.
- Traffic: baseline Poisson steady QPS, pulses: 500 RPS for 4s every 60s; echo probes: single request every 200ms to measure tail in-between bursts.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 latency (server-side), token/sec, batch size distribution, KVcache hit ratio, evictions/sec, CPU/GPU util.

Run matrix (quick):
- A: baseline steady 50 RPS, no pulses (control)
- B: pulses every 60s, 4s long, 500 RPS (default batch timeout 8ms)
- C: same as B but batch timeout = 3ms
- D: same as B but preemption disabled
- E: same as B but small cache budget (simulated higher eviction)

Observed (summary of key runs):
- Control (A): p99 ~ 72ms, p999 ~ 130ms, batch size avg 3.1
- B (pulse, 8ms): during pulse p99 spikes to ~1.2s, p999 to ~2.8s; after pulse an elevated tail persists ~18s before returning to baseline; KV hit ratio drops by ~12% during pulse and recovers slowly.
- C (timeout 3ms): pulse p99 reduced to ~850ms, p999 ~1.6s; recovery faster (~9–10s). Batch sizes skew smaller (avg 2.0) which reduced queuing but increased compute overhead.
- D (preemption off): worst behavior — p99 > 2s during pulse, p999 > 5s; interestingly recovery was faster (~12s) than B but with much higher immediate tail.
- E (low cache budget): p99 similar to B but recovery extended to ~35s; evictions/sec spiked and stayed elevated.

Lightweight ascii sighting (echo probe latency timeline, excerpt, ms):
T=0..8s (pulse): 40 48 120 350 900 1200 1400 1600 2000
T=9..30s (recovery): 180 150 140 130 120 115 110 95 85 80 78 75 74 ... back to 72
(These are noisy; but captures the long decay tail.)

Initial hypotheses & interpretations:
- Short batch timeout helps by cutting queuing amplification (less head-of-line amplification), but increases per-request compute overhead — tradeoff visible between p99 improvement and throughput efficiency.
- Preemption seems to reduce post-pulse tail persistence in some configs (B vs D) but increases instantaneous tail when on — likely because preemption yields work re-entrancy and additional scheduling overhead. Need finer tracing to confirm where stalls occur.
- Cache budget/evictions are a major factor in recovery time — thrashing keeps new requests cold. Consider a small TTL-based soft-probe (cheap probes to warm hot KV keys) immediately after pulse finishes.

Quick micro-actions to try next (prioritized):
1) Add a 'soft-probe' experiment: after each pulse, fire 20 low-cost warm probes to likely hot prefixes and measure delta recovery time. (A/B with/without)
2) Instrument batch formation timeline in runtime for a single node: record per-batch creation time, first-request-arrival vs dispatch to GPU, and preemption counts.
3) Re-run D with finer-grained preemption knob (max preemptions per second) — maybe current setting too aggressive.
4) Run longer duty-cycle test (pulses every 30s for 1hr) to observe steady-state thrash.
5) Explore adaptive batch timeout: scale timeout down during pulses. Implement simple rule in harness and compare.

Open questions / oddities to investigate:
- Why does disabling preemption increase instantaneous tail but sometimes reduce recovery length? Trace suggests preemption forces cancellation/repush which taxes batch warm caches.
- Are there kernel-level stalls (GPU io) when batch sizes suddenly spike? Need NVTX capture for a pulse run.
- Could client-side pacing (smoothing microbursts) be cheaper than server-side adaptive heuristics? Need cost model.

Notes to self / messy TODOs:
- Clean up bench/pulse-echo-v0 to emit JSON lines with fields: ts, req_id, batch_id, batch_size, queue_ms, gpu_ms, kv_hit (bool), preempted (bool).
- Add a small python viz to overlay KV hit ratio vs p99 (quick correlation).
- Slack thread: #eng-serving-runtime — post quick TL;DR + link to this doc and ask Maya to run soft-probe A/B.

Conclusions (early):
- Short: pulse -> echo decay exists and is dominated by KV cache thrash + batching behavior. Simple tuning (shorter timeout) helps but is not a silver bullet. Soft-probes and adaptive timeout policies are promising and cheap experiments to run next.

If I get time: push a tiny PR that implements a soft-probe flag in the harness (cheap), then re-run E and D configs with/without soft-probe.

End of scratchpad. This is messy by design — will formalize into a perf test spec if we see reproducible gains.
notes_brief: Personal scratch: pulse-echo microburst bench. Try soft-probes + adaptive timeout. Capture batch formation trace next.
